title: The Brain · Episode 1
chapters: Reflexes: when your spine decides first

units.t: The Brain. Episode one.
In this episode: How neurons talk, Reflexes: when your spine decides first and The science of pain.
Part one. How neurons talk.
Every thought, memory and movement comes down to cells sending electrical and chemical messages.
Here's how they do it.
Anatomy of a neuron.
A neuron has three main parts.
Branching dendrites receive signals.
The cell body combines those inputs.
A long, thin axon carries the output away, sometimes over a metre, like those from your lower spine to your toes.
Many axons are wrapped in myelin, a fatty insulating layer that speeds signals up enormously; the signal jumps between small gaps in the myelin.
The brain has around 86 billion neurons, a figure from careful cell-counting studies, plus a similar number of supporting glial cells.
Oligodendrocytes make myelin in the brain and spinal cord, and Schwann cells do so elsewhere.
Astrocytes help feed neurons, and microglia clear debris and prune unused synapses.
Glia means 'glue', but they take an active part.
The electrical signal.
A resting neuron keeps a small voltage across its membrane, about minus 70 millivolts, by pumping ions in and out.
When enough input pushes it past a threshold, channels open, sodium rushes in, and a spike of voltage, the action potential, races down the axon.
Potassium flows out to reset it.
It's all-or-nothing: a neuron either fires or it doesn't.
Stronger stimuli make neurons fire more often, not more strongly.
Signals in thin, unmyelinated fibres crawl at about a metre per second, while in myelinated axons they can travel over 100 metres per second.
Across the synapse.
Most neurons don't quite touch.
Between them is a synapse, far narrower than a human hair.
When an action potential arrives, the axon releases neurotransmitter molecules from vesicles.
They cross in a fraction of a millisecond and bind to receptors on the next neuron, making it more or less likely to fire.
Then they are broken down or recycled.
The brain has an estimated 100 trillion or more synapses.
Glutamate is the main excitatory neurotransmitter and GABA the main inhibitory one.
Each neuron adds up both to decide whether to fire.
Too much excitation can cause seizures.
Alcohol and some sedatives enhance GABA, slowing reactions.
Dopamine and serotonin act more like volume controls, tuning whole networks.
Wiring by use.
In 1949, psychologist Donald Hebb proposed that when one neuron repeatedly helps another fire, the connection strengthens.
It is often summarised as 'neurons that fire together, wire together'.
In 1973, researchers reported long-term potentiation in the hippocampus, a memory hub, where repeated stimulation made synapses stronger for hours or longer.
Practice physically strengthens pathways, adding receptors and even new connections, while unused connections can weaken and be pruned.
This is how skills and memories are built, and why regular practice and review beat a single long session.
Faults and interfaces.
In multiple sclerosis, the immune system attacks myelin, slowing signals.
Parkinson's disease involves loss of dopamine-producing neurons.
Alzheimer's disease damages synapses and neurons and involves abnormal protein build-ups.
Many medicines act at synapses; some antidepressants, for example, affect how serotonin is recycled.
Because neurons communicate electrically, activity can be recorded and decoded.
Brain-computer interfaces place sensors near the motor cortex and translate firing patterns into commands.
In trials in the early 2000s, people with paralysis learned to move a cursor by imagining moving a hand.
Melbourne company Synchron's Stentrode is threaded up the jugular vein beside the motor cortex, avoiding open brain surgery.
In a small Australian trial, recipients with motor neurone disease used it to text, shop and bank online.
It is still experimental.
The key idea: A neuron receives signals through dendrites and sends them along an axon, often insulated with myelin.
Part two. Reflexes: when your spine decides first.
Touch a hot pan and your hand is gone before you feel the pain.
That split-second move is made without your brain's permission.
Descartes and the fire.
René Descartes' Treatise of Man, published in 1664 after his death, included a famous drawing of a boy with his foot near a fire.
Descartes imagined that heat tugged on tiny threads in the nerves, opening valves in the brain that sent spirits to the muscles to pull the foot away.
The details were wrong, but the core idea was striking: some actions might happen mechanically, like clockwork, without any conscious choice.
Over the following centuries, scientists found that many automatic responses do not even need the brain.
They are handled lower down, in the spinal cord, by circuits we now call reflex arcs.
The knee jerk.
When a doctor taps the tendon below your kneecap, your lower leg kicks forward.
In 1875 two German neurologists, Wilhelm Erb and Carl Westphal, independently described this reflex, and it has been tested ever since.
The tap briefly stretches the quadriceps muscle at the front of the thigh.
Stretch sensors in the muscle, called muscle spindles, fire signals along a sensory nerve into the spinal cord.
There, the sensory neuron connects directly to a motor neuron, which sends a command straight back, telling the muscle to contract.
With only one connection in the chain, it is a monosynaptic reflex.
In everyday life it helps keep you upright.
Anatomy of a reflex.
A reflex arc has five basic parts.
A receptor detects a change such as stretch, heat or pressure.
A sensory neuron carries the signal to the spinal cord or brainstem.
A processing step links it to an outgoing motor neuron, sometimes through extra cells called interneurons.
Finally a muscle or gland responds.
British physiologist Charles Sherrington spent decades mapping these circuits and coined the word synapse for the gap between nerve cells.
He showed that reflexes coordinate muscles in pairs.
When the quadriceps contracts in the knee jerk, signals simultaneously relax the hamstrings behind the thigh so they do not fight the movement.
Sherrington shared the 1932 Nobel Prize.
Pulling back from danger.
Step on a sharp object and your foot lifts before you have time to think.
This withdrawal reflex is more complex than the knee jerk.
It uses several interneurons in the spinal cord to activate a group of muscles that pull the limb away.
At the same moment, a linked circuit called the crossed extensor reflex stiffens your other leg so it can take your weight and you do not topple.
Signals also travel up to the brain, which is why you then feel the pain, look down and perhaps say something unprintable.
The reflex circuit is short and conscious pain takes longer to form, so the movement often comes first.
Babies, speed and skill.
Newborn reflexes fade within months as the brain's higher regions take control.
Stroke a cheek and the baby turns to feed; touch a palm and they grip; sense a fall and they fling out their arms.
In 1896 Joseph Babinski described how stroking the sole makes the big toe curl down in healthy adults.
If it points up and the toes fan out, it can signal damage to nerve pathways from the brain.
A spinal reflex takes only a few tens of milliseconds.
A conscious reaction to something you see takes around a fifth to a quarter of a second.
In sprinting, a runner who reacts within a tenth of a second of the gun has false started, because a genuine response cannot reliably be that fast.
Catching a ball feels like a reflex but is learned.
The key idea: The idea that the body can react automatically goes back to Descartes, and we now know many reflexes are handled by the spinal cord.
Part three. The science of pain.
Pain feels like a simple signal from an injury, but it is really the brain's best guess about danger.
That surprising idea changes how we understand hurt.
A nail through the boot.
A case reported in the British Medical Journal in 1995 describes a builder who jumped onto a 15 centimetre nail.
It went straight through his boot and he was in agony, needing strong pain relief.
When doctors removed the boot, the nail had passed between his toes without touching his foot.
Other people suffer serious injuries in emergencies or sport and feel little at first.
Pain is not a direct readout of damage.
It is something the brain produces to protect you from what it judges to be a threat.
Nerve endings called nociceptors detect potential harm, such as intense pressure, heat, cold or chemicals from damaged tissue, and signal the spinal cord and brain.
That detection, nociception, is not the same as pain.
Context shapes pain.
Warning signals do not simply switch pain on.
Many brain regions weigh them against context, memories, attention, mood and expectations.
That is why the same injury can feel very different in different situations.
A paper cut on a stressful day may sting more than a scrape in an exciting footy match.
Anxiety and fear tend to amplify pain, while distraction and feeling safe can reduce it.
Stub your toe and you often feel a sharp first jolt, then a duller throb, as faster and slower nerve fibres deliver their messages in turn.
In phantom limb pain, people feel pain in an amputated limb because the brain's map of the body still includes it.
All pain is real, whatever its source.
Turning pain down.
Bang your elbow and you rub it without thinking.
In 1965, Ronald Melzack and Patrick Wall proposed gate control theory: circuits in the spinal cord act like a gate, letting more or fewer pain signals through.
Touch and pressure signals can partly close it, which is why rubbing helps.
The details have been revised, but the idea that the nervous system actively modulates pain remains influential.
In the 1970s, scientists found brain receptors for opium-derived drugs like morphine, because the body makes its own, including endorphins, endogenous plus morphine.
They dampen pain during stress, injury and exercise and play a role in some placebo effects.
Opioid medicines are powerful but can cause dependence, so Australia regulates them tightly.
When pain outstays its welcome.
Acute pain is the short-term pain of an injury and usually fades as tissue heals.
Chronic pain generally means pain lasting longer than about three months, and it is common.
Australian health organisations estimate around one in five adults lives with it.
In many cases the nervous system itself has changed, becoming more sensitive so it produces pain more easily, a process called central sensitisation.
The alarm system has become overprotective, sounding off even when the danger is small or gone.
This does not mean the pain is imagined.
Treating chronic pain often takes more than looking for ongoing damage, and may need to address the nervous system's sensitivity as well.
Living well with pain.
Understanding pain as a protective output of the brain has changed how many people are treated.

For persistent pain, care often combines several elements: graded physical activity that gradually builds confidence and capacity, good sleep, stress management, and pain education that explains how the nervous system works.
Psychological therapies can help reduce fear and restore valued activities.
Medicines still have a place, but for many types of chronic pain, relying on them alone tends to work less well than a combined approach.
Australian researchers have been prominent in pain education.
This is general information, not medical advice.
If you live with pain, talk to your GP.
healthdirect and Painaustralia are helpful starting points.
The key idea: Pain is produced by the brain and does not always match the amount of tissue damage.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What does the axon do?
Answer. Carries signals away from the cell body.
Question two. What do scientists now know about many automatic responses?
Answer. Many are handled in the spinal cord.
Question three. What did the case of the builder and the nail reveal?
Answer. Severe pain can occur with no injury.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
